passages.title: A History of the Umbrella
passages.body:
**A**  The umbrella is older than most people assume. Shade-giving parasols appear in Egyptian, Assyrian and Chinese art thousands of years ago, carried above rulers as symbols of status rather than protection from rain. The collapsible, rain-proof umbrella seems to have been developed in China, where oiled paper or waxed silk was stretched over a bamboo frame. By the tenth century these were common enough to appear in paintings and to be lent by inns to travellers.

**B**  Europe was slower to accept the device. Umbrellas reached Italy and France in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but early examples were heavy and expensive. In Paris they were first used by women as sunshades; men who carried them risked ridicule, since an umbrella was thought to suggest delicacy. The habit changed in the eighteenth century. Jonas Hanway, a British traveller and writer, is often credited as the first man to carry an umbrella regularly through the streets of London, in the 1750s, and he was mocked for it in the press.

**C**  The modern umbrella owes much to nineteenth-century engineering. In 1852 Samuel Fox, an English steelmaker, patented a frame of steel ribs that was lighter and stronger than the wooden or whalebone frames then in use. Combined with cheaper cotton covers and sewing machines, this made umbrellas affordable for ordinary households. Folding designs followed, and by the end of the century the umbrella had become an everyday object rather than a luxury.

**D**  Today the umbrella is so cheap that it is often treated as disposable. Millions are lost or abandoned each year, and the metal and plastic they contain rarely reach a recycling stream. Some cities have started repair cafés where broken umbrellas are mended, and a few manufacturers now sell models with replaceable canopies. The problem, designers argue, is not the umbrella itself but the assumption that it should cost less than a sandwich.
